papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a mechanism in Transformer-based LMs for arithmetic reasoning: information is transferred via attention to the last token and processed by late MLP modules to incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides empirical evidence that LMs process arithmetic queries by conveying information via attention to the last token, where late MLPs generate result-related information, and this mechanism is specific to arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Early MLP layers at operand tokens encode operand information, while attention modules transfer this information to the last token.
Late MLP modules at the last token encode result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
This activation pattern is specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
Fine-tuning on three-operand queries leads to the emergence of the late MLP activation site observed in two-operand settings.
Neuron-level interventions show that the circuits for arithmetic are distinct from those for other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The scope is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division).
Queries are synthetically-generated from natural language descriptions rather than real-life math word problems.
Attention modules are considered as a whole without analyzing individual attention heads.
future_direction: Studying a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expanding analysis to math-based queries in real-life settings.
Identifying specific attention heads responsible for information transfer.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy\n Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads to translation performance? Do they play consistent and interpretable roles? Can the number of heads be significantly reduced without serious performance loss?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that only a subset of attention heads are important for translation, with interpretable functions, and introduces a pruning method that can remove the majority of heads without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Specialized attention heads are most important for translation and can be identified, while many heads are redundant and can be pruned without serious performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small subset of attention heads are important for translation.
Important heads have specialized and interpretable functions, such as attending to adjacent tokens, specific syntactic relations, and rare words.
The proposed pruning method can remove the vast majority of heads (e.g., 38 out of 48 encoder heads) with only a small drop in BLEU (0.15).
Encoder self-attention heads are pruned first, while decoder-encoder attention heads are the most important.
Lower decoder layers retain self-attention heads for language modeling, while higher decoder layers retain decoder-encoder attention heads for conditioning on the source sentence.
papers.limitation: The impact of target language morphology on the accuracy of syntactic attention heads is not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate how the pruning method compares to alternative methods of model compression in neural machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Multi-head self-attention is a key component of the Transformer, a
state-of-the-art architecture for neural machine translation. In this work we
evaluate the contribution made by individual attention heads in the encoder to
the overall performance of the model and analyze the roles played by them. We
find that the most important and confident heads play consistent and often
linguistically-interpretable roles. When pruning heads using a method based on
stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty, we observe
that specialized heads are last to be pruned. Our novel pruning method removes
the vast majority of heads without seriously affecting performance. For
example, on the English-Russian WMT dataset, pruning 38 out of 48 encoder heads
results in a drop of only 0.15 BLEU.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: Evaluating self-attention interpretability through human-grounded experimental protocol
papers.research_question: How can attention coefficients from Transformers help in providing interpretability? The paper proposes a new attention-based interpretability method (CLS-A) and evaluates it against other methods using a human-grounded experiment.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new attention-based interpretability method called CLS-A, which computes word importance scores from the attention distribution of the classification (CLS) token. Through human experiments, it shows CLS-A performs comparably to established methods (SHAP, LIME) in aiding human annotation tasks and highlights a link between classifier prediction probability and explanation quality.
papers.conclusion: CLS-A is a valid interpretability method that performs as well as SHAP and LIME in human-grounded evaluations, confirming that self-attention contains rich information for explaining Transformer classifiers. Human-based experimental protocols are a relevant approach for evaluating interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
CLS-A performs comparably to SHAP and LIME in terms of average participant reaction time and accuracy in text annotation tasks.
CLS-A has a lower computational cost compared to other interpretability methods and is available by design within the classifier architecture.
There is a strong link between the probability score of a classifier's prediction and the quality of the explanation; higher probability scores lead to more relevant explanations.
Participants responded faster and more accurately when exposed to CLS-A compared to a random baseline, particularly for texts with high classifier confidence.
The study validates the relevance of using self-attention coefficients for explaining Transformer classifiers.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to binary classifiers.
future_direction: Analyzing multi-class classifiers to obtain more refined conclusions.
Including other feature importance methods, such as gradient-based approaches, in the comparison benchmark.
Building an experimental protocol to assess the quality of counterfactual explanations.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have played a crucial role in the development of complex architectures such as Transformers in natural language processing. However, Transformers remain hard to interpret and are considered as black-boxes. This paper aims to assess how attention coefficients from Transformers can help in providing interpretability. A new attention-based interpretability method called CLaSsification-Attention (CLS-A) is proposed. CLS-A computes an interpretability score for each word based on the attention coefficient distribution related to the part specific to the classification task within the Transformer architecture. A human-grounded experiment is conducted to evaluate and compare CLS-A to other interpretability methods. The experimental protocol relies on the capacity of an interpretability method to provide explanation in line with human reasoning. Experiment design includes measuring reaction times and correct response rates by human subjects. CLS-A performs comparably to usual interpretability methods regarding average participant reaction time and accuracy. The lower computational cost of CLS-A compared to other interpretability methods and its availability by design within the classifier make it particularly interesting. Data analysis also highlights the link between the probability score of a classifier prediction and adequate explanations. Finally, our work confirms the relevancy of the use of CLS-A and shows to which extent self-attention contains rich information to explain Transformer classifiers.

papers.title: Attention Interpretability Across NLP Tasks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the interpretability of attention weights in neural network models, specifically addressing when attention weights are interpretable and when they are not.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive explanation for when attention weights are interpretable, showing that attention is interpretable when it is essential for the model's prediction and cannot be reduced to a gating unit, and validates this through experiments on diverse NLP tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention weights are interpretable and correlated with feature importance measures when they are essential for the model's prediction and cannot be reduced to a gating unit.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights in single sequence tasks (like text classification) can be interpreted as a gating unit and are not interpretable as explanations.
For pair sequence and generation tasks, attention weights are crucial and interpretable.
Altering attention weights in single sequence tasks does not substantially affect performance, while in pair sequence and generation tasks it does.
Attention weights in single sequence tasks do not correlate well with feature importance measures, but they do in pair sequence and generation tasks.
Manual evaluation shows that attention weights in single sequence tasks do not provide a reason for the prediction, while in pair sequence tasks they do.
papers.abstract: The attention layer in a neural network model provides insights into the model's reasoning behind its prediction, which are usually criticized for being opaque. Recently, seemingly contradictory viewpoints have emerged about the interpretability of attention weights (Jain & Wallace, 2019; Vig & Belinkov, 2019). Amid such confusion arises the need to understand attention mechanism more systematically. In this work, we attempt to fill this gap by giving a comprehensive explanation which justifies both kinds of observations (i.e., when is attention interpretable and when it is not). Through a series of experiments on diverse NLP tasks, we validate our observations and reinforce our claim of interpretability of attention through manual evaluation.

papers.title: Disentangling Direction and Magnitude in Transformer Representations: A Double Dissociation Through L2-Matched Perturbation Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the distinct functional roles of direction (orientation) and magnitude (norm) in transformer hidden state representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L2-matched perturbation analysis to discover a double dissociation: angular perturbations disproportionately damage language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations disproportionately damage syntactic accuracy, with distinct mechanistic pathways through attention and LayerNorm.
papers.conclusion: Direction and magnitude serve partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm-based transformers: direction preferentially governs attentional routing, while magnitude encodes structural position and modulates processing intensity through LayerNorm.
papers.key_findings:
Angular perturbations cause up to 42.9× more damage to language modeling loss than magnitude perturbations at equal Euclidean displacement.
Magnitude perturbations cause up to 20.4% greater drop in syntactic accuracy (subject-verb agreement) than angular perturbations.
Causal intervention shows angular damage is substantially mediated by attention pathways (28.4% recovery via repair), while magnitude damage is substantially mediated by LayerNorm pathways (29.9% recovery).
The dissociation pattern replicates across scales within the Pythia architecture family but reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures like TinyLlama.
Magnitude correlates with parse tree depth, and disrupting this correlation explains why magnitude perturbations specifically impair syntactic processing.
papers.limitation:
L2 matching assumes equal Euclidean distance makes perturbations comparable, but neural networks operate in anisotropic spaces; angular perturbations amplify 3× more than magnitude by the final layer.
Angular perturbations use random orthogonal directions; results might differ for systematic rotations toward known feature directions.
Findings are specific to the Pythia/OPT architecture family and do not generalize to all transformers; the pattern reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures (TinyLlama).
Only middle layers (8–15) were targeted for intervention; early and late layers may show different patterns.
Syntactic evaluation is limited to subject-verb agreement from BLiMP; other syntactic phenomena may show different patterns.
Causal repair experiments account for only ~30% of each perturbation's damage; the remaining ~70% likely flows through MLP layers and residual connections.
future_direction: Feature-specific rotations (systematic rotations toward/away from known feature directions).
Investigating how the roles of direction and magnitude evolve during training.
Exploring magnitude as a confidence signal for uncertainty quantification.
Extending the methodology to other modalities (e.g., vision transformers).
Systematic comparison across normalization schemes (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm).
papers.abstract: Transformer hidden states encode information as high-dimensional vectors, yet whether direction (orientation in representational space) and magnitude (vector norm) serve distinct functional roles remains unclear. Studying Pythia-family models, we discover a striking cross-over dissociation: angular perturbations cause up to 42.9 more damage to language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations cause disproportionately more damage to syntactic processing (20.4% vs.1.6% accuracy drop on subject-verb agreement).This finding is enabled by L2-matched perturbation analysis, a methodology ensuring that an gular and magnitude perturbations achieve identical Euclidean displacements. Causal intervention reveals that angular damage flows substantially through the attention pathways (28.4% loss recovery via attention repair), while magnitude damage flows partly through the LayerNorm pathways(29.9% recovery via LayerNorm repair). These patterns replicate across scales within the Pythia architecture family. These findings provide evidence that direction and magnitude support partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm based architectures. The direction preferentially affects attentional routing, while magnitude modulates processing intensity for fine-grained syntactic judgments. We find different patterns in RMSNorm-based architectures, suggesting that the dissociation depends on architectural choices. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis and have implications for model editing and interpretability research

papers.title: From Balustrades to Pierre Vinken: Looking for Syntax in Transformer\n Self-Attentions
papers.research_question: Does the Transformer encoder self-attention capture syntactic structures, and to what extent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a transparent, linguistically uninformed algorithm to extract constituency trees from self-attention patterns (balustrades) and shows that Transformer encoders do capture syntactic information.
papers.conclusion: Syntax is indeed captured in the self-attentions of Transformer encoders, and the proposed method can extract syntactic trees without using annotated data.
papers.key_findings:
Self-attention heads in Transformer encoders frequently exhibit baluster patterns (sequences of consecutive states attending to the same position) that resemble syntactic phrases.
Constituency trees extracted from these balusters using a deterministic CKY-based algorithm show higher precision and recall against standard parse trees than uninformed baselines, indicating the presence of syntactic information.
Not all attention heads are syntactic; selecting a subset of heads (via a greedy addition method) improves the quality of the extracted trees.
The extracted trees are more similar to the flatter, more balanced trees of German and French treebanks than to the strongly right-branching English Penn Treebank.
The first encoder layer contributes about one third of the selected syntactic heads, while the last two layers each contribute about one fifth.
papers.limitation:
The automatic evaluation only assesses whether extracted structures match the specific syntactic formalism of the standard treebank, and cannot appreciate alternative structures that may also be syntactically valid.
The encoder may not capture a full syntactic tree because it is trained for machine translation, which may not require all syntactic structures.
The tree extraction algorithm uses all attention heads, including non-syntactic ones, which may introduce incorrect structures.
future_direction: Investigate alternative syntactic formalisms that might better match the structures captured by the encoder, such as flat structures or partially overlapping phrases.
Further analysis of the syntactic heads and their distribution across layers.
papers.abstract:
We inspect the multi-head self-attention in Transformer NMT encoders for
three source languages, looking for patterns that could have a syntactic
interpretation. In many of the attention heads, we frequently find sequences of
consecutive states attending to the same position, which resemble syntactic
phrases. We propose a transparent deterministic method of quantifying the
amount of syntactic information present in the self-attentions, based on
automatically building and evaluating phrase-structure trees from the
phrase-like sequences. We compare the resulting trees to existing constituency
treebanks, both manually and by computing precision and recall.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: CRANE: Causal Relevance Analysis of Language-Specific Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are language capabilities organized at the neuron level in multilingual LLMs? The paper redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity and proposes a method to identify language-specific neurons.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CRANE, a relevance-based framework for identifying language-specific neurons by functional necessity, and finds asymmetric, language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations in multilingual LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CRANE provides a framework for studying language-specific neurons based on functional necessity, revealing that language-specific neurons are language-selective but non-exclusive, and highlighting the importance of distinguishing statistical correlation from functional contribution.
papers.key_findings:
CRANE induces targeted functional degradation on the intended language while preserving performance on non-target languages, outperforming activation-based methods like LAPE.
Neuron-level interventions reveal an asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations.
Normalized kurtosis of relevance distributions reveals language-related structure in neuron contributions.
Neuron sets identified on the Base model retain functional influence when transferred to the Chat model, indicating partial preservation of language-specific neurons after instruction tuning.
The proposed LangSpec-F1 metric quantifies language-selective functional effects under neuron intervention.
papers.limitation:
CRANE currently relies on normalized kurtosis to characterize concentration patterns in language-conditioned relevance distributions, which is only one possible statistic.
Functional validation is performed via neuron masking, a relatively coarse intervention; more fine-grained causal techniques may provide deeper insight.
Experiments focus on three languages and a single model family, and open-ended generation evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge protocol which may introduce variance.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to broader language coverage, additional architectures, and alternative evaluation paradigms.
Using more fine-grained causal techniques, such as neuron re-weighting or path-specific analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across languages, yet how language capabilities are organized at the neuron level remains poorly understood. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. We propose CRANE, a relevance-based analysis framework that redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity, identifying language-specific neurons through targeted neuron-level interventions. CRANE characterizes neuron specialization by their contribution to language-conditioned predictions rather than activation magnitude. Our implementation will be made publicly available. Neuron-level interventions reveal a consistent asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages to a substantial extent, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations. Experiments on English, Chinese, and Vietnamese across multiple benchmarks, together with a dedicated relevance-based metric and base-to-chat model transfer analysis, show that CRANE isolates language-specific components more precisely than activation-based methods.

papers.title: Using Mechanistic Interpretability to Craft Adversarial Attacks against Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to craft practical adversarial inputs (jailbreaks) for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Subspace Rerouting (SSR), a white-box adversarial attack method that uses mechanistic interpretability to efficiently jailbreak LLMs by rerouting embeddings to acceptance subspaces.
papers.conclusion: SSR is an effective adversarial attack framework that operationalizes mechanistic interpretability insights, and it also serves as a practical interpretability tool that operates within the model's natural processing pathways.
papers.key_findings:
SSR achieves high attack success rates (80-95%) on state-of-the-art aligned LLMs.
SSR is computationally efficient, generating jailbreaks in seconds to minutes.
Harmful and harmless content is linearly separable in the activation space of aligned LLMs, a property SSR exploits.
SSR can produce interpretable adversarial tokens (e.g., 'responsibly', 'ethical').
SSR can be used as an interpretability tool (e.g., reverse-lens to find inputs that trigger specific features).
papers.limitation:
The causal nature of autoregressive transformers limits perturbations to influencing only subsequent token representations.
SSR optimisation may affect multiple components simultaneously, making component attribution difficult.
Prefix-based or long perturbations can alter the entire context and change the semantic meaning of the instruction, leading to failed jailbreaks.
The attack has many hyperparameters, making comprehensive ablation studies impractical and reproducibility challenging.
SSR attacks show extremely poor transfer rates between models.
future_direction: Combining SSR with more constrained optimisation objectives to isolate specific causal mechanisms.
Using perplexity in the loss function to improve transfer rates of attacks.
Comparing SSR with other mechanistic interpretability tools on established benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Traditional white-box methods for creating adversarial perturbations against LLMs typically rely only on gradient computation from the targeted model, ignoring the internal mechanisms responsible for attack success or failure. Conversely, interpretability studies that analyze these internal mechanisms lack practical applications beyond runtime interventions. We bridge this gap by introducing a novel white-box approach that leverages mechanistic interpretability techniques to craft practical adversarial inputs. Specifically, we first identify acceptance subspaces - sets of feature vectors that do not trigger the model's refusal mechanisms - then use gradient-based optimization to reroute embeddings from refusal subspaces to acceptance subspaces, effectively achieving jailbreaks. This targeted approach significantly reduces computation cost, achieving attack success rates of 80-95\% on state-of-the-art models including Gemma2, Llama3.2, and Qwen2.5 within minutes or even seconds, compared to existing techniques that often fail or require hours of computation. We believe this approach opens a new direction for both attack research and defense development. Furthermore, it showcases a practical application of mechanistic interpretability where other methods are less efficient, which highlights its utility. The code and generated datasets are available at https://github.com/Sckathach/subspace-rerouting.

papers.title: Enhancing Multilingual Text Understanding viaTransformer-Based Meta-Learning
papers.research_question: How can multilingual text understanding be enhanced by integrating structured linguistic knowledge (syntactic and semantic) into transformer-based models via meta-learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel framework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning via a Grammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, enhancing multilingual text understanding by aligning neural attention mechanisms with syntactic dependencies.
papers.conclusion: The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA into a transformer-based meta-learning framework significantly improves multilingual text understanding, though limitations exist in handling noisy language and reliance on syntactic annotations.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model (LexiStruct with GIRA) outperforms baseline methods on multiple multilingual benchmarks (XNLI, MLDoc, TyDiQAt, WikiAnn) across metrics like NDCG, Recall, MRR, and Hit Rate.
Ablation studies show that key components (Syntactic Structure Injection, Syntax-Semantics Alignment, Grammar-Semantics Alignment) are essential for the model's performance, with removal of any leading to significant drops in metrics.
The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA improves the model's robustness and interpretability in multilingual understanding tasks.
papers.limitation:
The integration of grammatical constraints may reduce the model's flexibility in handling less-structured or noisy language inputs, such as colloquialisms or code-switching phenomena.
The current implementation assumes access to high-quality syntactic annotations, which may not be available for all languages, especially low-resource ones.
future_direction: Explore strategies for relaxing the assumption of high-quality syntactic annotations, possibly through unsupervised or semi-supervised learning of syntactic structures.
Extend the model's adaptability to more diverse and informal language domains to improve broader applicability in real-world multilingual settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> In the evolving landscape of computational sciences, the integration of structured linguistic knowledge into deep learningmodels has become increasingly vital for advancing multilingual text understanding. Traditional transformer-based architectures,while powerful, often lack the capacity to inherently capture the syntactic and semantic nuances present across diverselanguages, leading to limitations in generalization and interpretability. To address these challenges, we introduce a novelframework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning. Our approach employsa structure-aware neural language model that incorporates grammatical constraints directly into the learning process,enhancing the model’s ability to comprehend and process multilingual data effectively. Central to our methodology is theGrammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, which aligns neural attention mechanisms with syntacticdependencies, ensuring that the model’s internal representations adhere to linguistic structures. Experimental evaluationsdemonstrate that our model achieves superior performance in multilingual understanding tasks, exhibiting enhanced robustnessinterpretability. This work contributes to the field by offering a principled method that bridges the gap between statistical learningand linguistic theory, aligning with the journal’s commitment to advancing both fundamental and applied computational sciences.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Why transformers are obviously good models of language
papers.research_question: Why are transformers effective models of language, and how do they align with theoretical perspectives on language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers are good models of language because their architecture, such as word embeddings and attention mechanisms, aligns with cognitive linguistic theories like prototype theory and construction grammar.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are effective models of language, and their alignment with certain linguistic theories suggests that these theories, such as those from cognitive linguistics, are correct.
papers.key_findings:
Word embeddings in transformers represent prototypical meanings of words, similar to Rosch's prototype theory.
Contextualized word meanings are constructed through self-attention layers, updating prototypes based on context.
Transformers can handle syntax and top-down processing via attention heads and skip connections, analogous to construction grammar.
Transformers lack a bias for local dependencies, allowing them to learn rare long-distance dependencies effectively.
The empirical success of transformers supports cognitive linguistic approaches over traditional syntactic theories.
papers.limitation:
Transformers assert false facts with the same degree of authority as true information.
Transformers have myopia in social contexts, such as not remembering past interactions in chatbots.
papers.abstract: Nobody knows how language works, but many theories abound. Transformers are a class of neural networks that process language automatically with more success than alternatives, both those based on neural computations and those that rely on other (e.g. more symbolic) mechanisms. Here, I highlight direct connections between the transformer architecture and certain theoretical perspectives on language. The empirical success of transformers relative to alternative models provides circumstantial evidence that the linguistic approaches that transformers embody should be, at least, evaluated with greater scrutiny by the linguistics community and, at best, considered to be the currently best available theories.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Sequence Continuation: Analyzing Shared Circuits in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models re-use shared circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, such as Arabic numerals, number words, and months.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that large language models re-use shared sub-circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, and shows that these circuits have analogous functionality across different models like GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformers leverage shared computational structures across similar tasks, advancing the understanding of how they represent abstract concepts and contributing to mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Shared sub-circuits exist for similar sequence continuation tasks in both GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B.
Key components include attention heads for sequence member detection (e.g., head 4.4) and successor prediction (e.g., head 9.1), as well as MLP 9 for next member calculation.
These circuits affect a wide range of math-related prompts, including intervaled sequences and arithmetic tasks.
The functionality of components is consistent across tasks, indicating re-use of computational structures.
Analogous sub-circuits are found in different models, suggesting common mechanisms for sequence processing.
future_direction: Examine if shared circuits appear in more models
Expand studies on non-linear features and their effects on math-related circuits
papers.abstract: While transformer models exhibit strong capabilities on linguistic tasks, their complex architectures make them difficult to interpret. Recent work has aimed to reverse engineer transformer models into human-readable representations called circuits that implement algorithmic functions. We extend this research by analyzing and comparing circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, which include increasing sequences of Arabic numerals, number words, and months. By applying circuit interpretability analysis, we identify a key sub-circuit in both GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B responsible for detecting sequence members and for predicting the next member in a sequence. Our analysis reveals that semantically related sequences rely on shared circuit subgraphs with analogous roles. Additionally, we show that this sub-circuit has effects on various math-related prompts, such as on intervaled circuits, Spanish number word and months continuation, and natural language word problems. Overall, documenting shared computational structures enables better model behavior predictions, identification of errors, and safer editing procedures. This mechanistic understanding of transformers is a critical step towards building more robust, aligned, and interpretable language models.

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: Contributions of Transformer Attention Heads in Multi- and Cross-lingual Tasks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer-based models on cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and how can important heads be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pruning a subset of attention heads in multilingual Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-R) generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and introduces a gradient-based method to rank and identify which heads to prune.
papers.conclusion: Pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer models generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and the gradient-based method effectively identifies heads to prune, offering better model interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning attention heads in mBERT and XLM-R generally has positive effects on model performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF).
A gradient-based method can effectively rank attention heads by importance, and pruning the lowest-ranked heads leads to performance improvements.
The important attention heads for a task are shared across languages, as evidenced by high correlation in head rankings across different languages.
Pruning attention heads is beneficial even when training data in the target language is limited, making models more applicable to resource-poor languages.
In multi-source language settings, pruning attention heads also improves performance, and the gradient-based ranking method can be extended to multiple source languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF) and may not generalize to other cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Improving model interpretability in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, e.g., XNLI and other passage-level classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Weicheng Ma, Kai Zhang, Renze Lou, Lili Wang, Soroush Vosoughi. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
papers.research_question: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? The paper proposes a benchmark to provide a basis for comparisons.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MIB, a benchmark for mechanistic interpretability with two tracks (circuit localization and causal variable localization) to enable meaningful comparisons of interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: MIB provides a standardized benchmark for comparing mechanistic interpretability methods, enabling meaningful evaluations and demonstrating progress in the field.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization.
Supervised Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) performs best on causal variable localization.
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are not better than non-featurized hidden vectors (neurons) for causal variable localization.
MIB enables meaningful comparisons and shows real progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The set of models and tasks is incomplete, limiting generalizability.
The metrics may not capture all aspects of interpretability that researchers care about.
The benchmark focuses on localization and featurization, leaving out other mechanistic interpretability goals like editing or control.
future_direction: Expand MIB to include more models and tasks.
Develop more comprehensive metrics that capture other aspects of interpretability.
Extend the benchmark to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components - and connections between them - most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable localization track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAE features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

papers.title: Structure Development in List-Sorting Transformers
papers.research_question: How do neural networks develop organized internal structures as they learn? The paper answers this for a single-layer attention-only transformer model trained on sorting lists of numbers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows how a one-layer attention-only transformer develops organized internal structures (vocabulary-splitting and copy-suppression) while learning to sort lists, and identifies training data characteristics (distribution of gaps between sorted list elements) as a key driver of these specializations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how developmental interpretability can reveal the emergence of structured solutions in transformers, with training data characteristics playing a crucial role in determining the type of specialization that develops.
papers.key_findings:
The model undergoes distinct developmental stages: initial learning, head-overlapping, vocabulary-splitting, and sometimes copy-suppression.
Vocabulary-splitting represents a simpler solution (as measured by the Local Learning Coefficient) and occurs even without weight decay, suggesting neural networks have an inherent bias toward simpler solutions.
Copy-suppression arises in some settings and functions to calibrate the copying head, increasing model confidence in this case.
The distribution of gaps (δ) between adjacent list elements in the training data drives the type of head specialization: smaller mean δ and lower variance favor copy-suppression, while larger variance favors vocabulary-splitting.
The model's internal organization is shaped by features of the training data, providing a concrete example of how data influences learned structures.
papers.limitation: The study uses a toy model, which limits the direct applicability to larger models.
papers.abstract: We study how a one-layer attention-only transformer develops relevant structures while learning to sort lists of numbers. At the end of training, the model organizes its attention heads in two main modes that we refer to as vocabulary-splitting and copy-suppression. Both represent simpler modes than having multiple heads handle overlapping ranges of numbers. Interestingly, vocabulary-splitting is present regardless of whether we use weight decay, a common regularization technique thought to drive simplification, supporting the thesis that neural networks naturally prefer simpler solutions. We relate copy-suppression to a mechanism in GPT-2 and investigate its functional role in our model. Guided by insights from a developmental analysis of the model, we identify features in the training data that drive the model's final acquired solution. This provides a concrete example of how the training data shape the internal organization of transformers, paving the way for future studies that could help us better understand how LLMs develop their internal structures.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Circuit Compositions: Exploring Modular Structures in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the modularity of neural networks by analyzing circuits for compositional subtasks, and whether functionally similar circuits can be composed to represent more complex capabilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation pruning through continuous sparsification for automatic circuit discovery, analyzes the modularity of circuits for compositional tasks, and shows that circuits can be composed via set operations to represent more complex functions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a method for circuit discovery and shows that transformer-based models exhibit modularity, with circuits for related tasks sharing nodes and being composable to handle more complex operations.
papers.key_findings:
Activation pruning through continuous sparsification successfully identifies faithful and minimal circuits for each string-edit subtask.
Functionally similar circuits exhibit significant node overlap and cross-task faithfulness.
Circuits can be combined through set operations (e.g., union) to create subnetworks that perform tasks beyond the original circuits.
The copy circuit is sparse and relies heavily on cross-attention modules, while binary circuits like prepend are larger and more complex.
Circuits identified via mean ablation are more faithful than those via zero ablation, and the ablation paradigm affects the identified nodes.
papers.limitation:
The method does not guarantee completeness of the identified circuits.
The choice of ablation value (mean vs zero) affects the identified circuits, indicating a dependence on the ablation paradigm.
The study is limited to a small model and synthetic dataset, and may not generalize to larger models and more diverse tasks.
future_direction: Incorporate completeness into the optimization framework for circuit discovery.
Scale the approach to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: A fundamental question in interpretability research is to what extent neural networks, particularly language models, implement reusable functions through subnetworks that can be composed to perform more complex tasks. Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have made progress in identifying $\textit{circuits}$, which represent the minimal computational subgraphs responsible for a model's behavior on specific tasks. However, most studies focus on identifying circuits for individual tasks without investigating how functionally similar circuits $\textit{relate}$ to each other. To address this gap, we study the modularity of neural networks by analyzing circuits for highly compositional subtasks within a transformer-based language model. Specifically, given a probabilistic context-free grammar, we identify and compare circuits responsible for ten modular string-edit operations. Our results indicate that functionally similar circuits exhibit both notable node overlap and cross-task faithfulness. Moreover, we demonstrate that the circuits identified can be reused and combined through set operations to represent more complex functional model capabilities.

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Contextual Counting: A Mechanistic Study of Transformers on a Quantitative Task
papers.research_question: How do Transformers, particularly with different positional encodings and causal structures, perform on a quantitative contextual counting task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the contextual counting task as a toy problem for interpretability, showing causal Transformers with no positional encoding perform best, and generalization depends on which tokens are used as bias terms.
papers.conclusion: The contextual counting task provides insights into Transformer interpretability in quantitative settings, showing causal models and specific positional encodings lead to better performance and revealing how generalization depends on bias token usage.
papers.key_findings:
Causal Transformers significantly outperform non-causal Transformers on the contextual counting task.
No positional encoding (NoPE) leads to the best accuracy, though rotary embeddings (RoPE) are competitive and easier to train.
Different solution classes exist with varying generalization performance to out-of-distribution sequence lengths and number of regions.
Generalization performance is linked to which tokens (e.g., BoS, delimiter, zero tokens) the model uses as bias terms.
The best-performing models implement a circuit where the encoder tags 1-tokens with contextual position and the decoder attends only to 1-tokens in the relevant region.
papers.limitation: The work does not explore what causes training to find one solution over another or how to improve the chances of finding generalizable solutions via SGD.
future_direction: Understanding what causes training regimens to find generalizable solutions and how to improve the likelihood of such solutions.
papers.abstract: Transformers have revolutionized machine learning across diverse domains, yet understanding their behavior remains crucial, particularly in high-stakes applications. This paper introduces the contextual counting task, a novel toy problem aimed at enhancing our understanding of Transformers in quantitative and scientific contexts. This task requires precise localization and computation within datasets, akin to object detection or region-based scientific analysis. We present theoretical and empirical analysis using both causal and non-causal Transformer architectures, investigating the influence of various positional encodings on performance and interpretability. In particular, we find that causal attention is much better suited for the task, and that no positional embeddings lead to the best accuracy, though rotary embeddings are competitive and easier to train. We also show that out of distribution performance is tightly linked to which tokens it uses as a bias term.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms.
