Our findings reveal that middle layers (particularly 2, 3, and 5) exhibit the most dramatic changes, with 62% of attention heads showing decreased entropy, indicating a shift toward focused information selection. We demonstrate that targeted LoRA adaptation of these identified circuits achieves significant performance improvement over standard LoRA fine-tuning while requiring fewer training epochs. This work bridges the gap between black-box evaluation and mechanistic understanding, providing insights into how neural networks perform information selection and compression during summarization.

papers.title: Start Making Sense(s): A Developmental Probe of Attention Specialization Using Lexical Ambiguity
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in Transformer language models develop specialized attention patterns for word sense disambiguation, and how robust are these heads to stimulus perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a developmental pipeline to probe attention specialization in Transformer LMs, using lexical ambiguity to identify and causally validate attention heads involved in word sense disambiguation, finding that larger models have more robust disambiguation heads.
papers.conclusion: Disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which are highly sensitive to cue position and part-of-speech (especially in smaller models), while larger models contain more robust disambiguation heads, highlighting the value of a developmental perspective in probing LM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Disambiguation performance improves with model size but with diminishing returns, with 410M achieving 92% of the performance of 12B despite having 3% as many parameters.
Inflection points in disambiguation performance occur early in pre-training (e.g., at steps 1000 and 2000).
In Pythia-14M, specific attention heads (e.g., (3,1) and (3,2)) show attention patterns that covary with disambiguation performance.
In Pythia-410M, multiple heads across layers show robust disambiguation behavior, generalizing across stimulus perturbations like positional and part-of-speech changes.
Ablating identified heads causally impairs disambiguation performance, especially in Pythia-14M, confirming their functional role.
papers.abstract: Despite an in-principle understanding of self-attention matrix operations in Transformer language models (LMs), it remains unclear precisely how these operations map onto interpretable computations or functions--and how or when individual attention heads develop specialized attention patterns. Here, we present a pipeline to systematically probe attention mechanisms, and we illustrate its value by leveraging lexical ambiguity--where a single word has multiple meanings--to isolate attention mechanisms that contribute to word sense disambiguation. We take a "developmental" approach: first, using publicly available Pythia LM checkpoints, we identify inflection points in disambiguation performance for each LM in the suite; in 14M and 410M, we identify heads whose attention to disambiguating words covaries with overall disambiguation performance across development. We then stress-test the robustness of these heads to stimulus perturbations: in 14M, we find limited robustness, but in 410M, we identify multiple heads with surprisingly generalizable behavior. Then, in a causal analysis, we find that ablating the target heads demonstrably impairs disambiguation performance, particularly in 14M. We additionally reproduce developmental analyses of 14M across all of its random seeds. Together, these results suggest: that disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which (especially in 14M) are highly sensitive to the position and part-of-speech of the disambiguating cue; and that larger models (410M) may contain heads with more robust disambiguation behavior. They also join a growing body of work that highlights the value of adopting a developmental perspective when probing LM mechanisms.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: Do Attention Heads in BERT Track Syntactic Dependencies?
papers.research_question: Do attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa implicitly capture syntactic dependency relations?
papers.core_contribution: Some attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa specialize in tracking specific syntactic dependency types, but no single head performs holistic parsing well, and fine-tuning has limited impact on attention patterns.
papers.conclusion: Certain specialist attention heads track specific dependency types, but no generalist heads exist for holistic parsing, and fine-tuning does not significantly change attention patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Some attention heads capture dependency types like nsubj and obj with high accuracy compared to baselines.
No attention head forms complete parse trees effectively, as shown by the MST method.
Fine-tuning on MNLI improves accuracy for long-distance clausal dependencies but degrades short-distance ones.
Fine-tuning on CoLA does not significantly affect dependency tracking accuracy.
Attention weights do not fully reflect the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.
papers.limitation:
Analyzing attention weights directly may not reveal much of the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.
Using the gold root in the MST method may artificially improve results, though bias is applied evenly.
papers.abstract: We investigate the extent to which individual attention heads in pretrained transformer language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, implicitly capture syntactic dependency relations. We employ two methods---taking the maximum attention weight and computing the maximum spanning tree---to extract implicit dependency relations from the attention weights of each layer/head, and compare them to the ground-truth Universal Dependency (UD) trees. We show that, for some UD relation types, there exist heads that can recover the dependency type significantly better than baselines on parsed English text, suggesting that some self-attention heads act as a proxy for syntactic structure. We also analyze BERT fine-tuned on two datasets---the syntax-oriented CoLA and the semantics-oriented MNLI---to investigate whether fine-tuning affects the patterns of their self-attention, but we do not observe substantial differences in the overall dependency relations extracted using our methods. Our results suggest that these models have some specialist attention heads that track individual dependency types, but no generalist head that performs holistic parsing significantly better than a trivial baseline, and that analyzing attention weights directly may not reveal much of the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Verb Conjugation in Transformers Is Determined by Linear Encodings of Subject Number
papers.research_question: Are linguistic features, specifically subject number, represented in a linear, interpretable format in transformer language models, and how does BERT use this information for verb conjugation?
papers.core_contribution: BERT's ability to conjugate verbs relies on a linear encoding of subject number that can be manipulated via causal intervention to predictably change conjugation behavior.
papers.conclusion: BERT uses a linear, interpretable encoding of subject number for verb conjugation, and this encoding's location changes across layers and positions depending on the presence of redundant cues.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's verb conjugation is determined by a linear encoding of subject number.
The linear encoding originates in the subject position at the embedding layer and moves to the verb position at the final layer.
When redundant cues to subject number exist, the encoding is distributed across multiple positions at middle layers.
Intervention on the number subspace can reverse conjugation accuracy (from 91.7% correct to 84.6% incorrect).
The encoding is specific to number; intervention does not affect perplexity for number-neutral words.
papers.limitation:
The dataset uses a uniform syntactic template, so results may not generalize to more naturalistic settings where verb conjugation may be conditioned by other factors.
The method cannot prove that BERT does not use a linear encoding for a feature when the intervention fails.
future_direction: Applying the causal intervention method to study what other kinds of features may have similarly strong linear encodings.
papers.abstract: Deep architectures such as Transformers are sometimes criticized for having uninterpretable "black-box" representations. We use causal intervention analysis to show that, in fact, some linguistic features are represented in a linear, interpretable format. Specifically, we show that BERT's ability to conjugate verbs relies on a linear encoding of subject number that can be manipulated with predictable effects on conjugation accuracy. This encoding is found in the subject position at the first layer and the verb position at the last layer, but distributed across positions at middle layers, particularly when there are multiple cues to subject number.

papers.title: Do Transformers know symbolic rules, and would we know if they did?
papers.research_question: Do Transformers internalize genuine symbolic rules, and how can we distinguish symbolic rule use from associative pattern matching?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that Transformers may function as the processor component within a larger symbolic architecture that uses input and output as external memory, and experimentally shows that generalization for abstract rules is significantly stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in classification tasks.
papers.conclusion: The question of whether Transformers internalize symbolic rules remains open, but the full input-Transformer-output pipeline can satisfy the architectural criterion of symbolicity by using attention and positional encoding for location-based memory addressing.
papers.key_findings:
T5 demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization across vocabularies in all tested tasks.
In vocabulary flip settings, T5 completely fails at classification tasks without data mixing, but achieves moderate success in sequence-to-sequence tasks even without mixing.
Repetition detection remains difficult for T5 even with mixed data, indicating a specific obstacle to learning abstract rules when associative heuristics are unavailable.
Generalization is systematically stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in comparable classification tasks.
The results highlight the challenge of conclusively attributing symbolic rule internalization to Transformers due to the unfalsifiability of non-symbolic explanations.
papers.limitation:
The experimental setup is simple and artificial, using artificial vocabularies of single characters and restricting the model architecture to T5.
The classification tasks are restricted to binary targets, and experiments are limited to a single Transformer variant.
future_direction: Examine the performance of tokens with more prevalent linguistic functions and compare different linguistic classes and languages in multilingual models.
Expand experiments to multi-class and multi-label settings, and to more Transformer variants and hyperparameters.
Investigate whether non-symbolic associative explanations for zero-shot success on identical token detection are plausible in practice.
papers.abstract: To improve the explainability of leading Transformer networks used in NLP, it is important to tease apart genuine symbolic rules from merely associative input-output patterns. However, we identify several inconsistencies in how ``symbolicity'' has been construed in recent NLP literature. To mitigate this problem, we propose two criteria to be the most relevant, one pertaining to a system's internal architecture and the other to the dissociation between abstract rules and specific input identities. From this perspective, we critically examine prior work on the symbolic capacities of Transformers, and deem the results to be fundamentally inconclusive for reasons inherent in experiment design. We further maintain that there is no simple fix to this problem, since it arises -- to an extent -- in all end-to-end settings. Nonetheless, we emphasize the need for more robust evaluation of whether non-symbolic explanations exist for success in seemingly symbolic tasks. To facilitate this, we experiment on four sequence modelling tasks on the T5 Transformer in two experiment settings: zero-shot generalization, and generalization across class-specific vocabularies flipped between the training and test set. We observe that T5's generalization is markedly stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in comparable classification tasks. Based on this, we propose a thus far overlooked analysis, where the Transformer itself does not need to be symbolic to be part of a symbolic architecture as the processor, operating on the input and output as external memory components.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Inferring Functionality of Attention Heads from their Parameters
papers.research_question: How to infer the functionality of attention heads in LLMs from their parameters without model training or inference, and to map how strongly heads implement predefined operations or to infer salient operations of a given head.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MAPS, a framework to infer attention head functionality directly from parameters, enabling mapping of predefined operations across heads and automatic characterization of salient operations.
papers.conclusion: Introduces MAPS, an efficient framework for inferring attention heads’ functionality from their parameters, and showcases its utility in systematically mapping functionality across the model and automatically characterizing salient operations of a given head.
papers.key_findings:
MAPS estimations correlate with head outputs during inference and are causally linked to model predictions.
MAPS reveals attention heads of certain operations that were overlooked in previous studies.
MAPS provides insights on function universality and architecture biases in LLMs.
Automatic pipeline produces plausible operation descriptions for most heads, as assessed by human judgment.
Heads often implement multiple relations, and smaller models tend to encode more relations per head.
papers.limitation: The automatic description pipeline sometimes hallucinates patterns not present in the mappings.
future_direction: Improve the automatic description pipeline to reduce hallucinations by using confidence aggregation, intrinsic classifiers, or NLI models.
papers.abstract: Attention heads are one of the building blocks of large language models (LLMs). Prior work on investigating their operation mostly focused on analyzing their behavior during inference for specific circuits or tasks. In this work, we seek a comprehensive mapping of the operations they implement in a model. We propose MAPS (Mapping Attention head ParameterS), an efficient framework that infers the functionality of attention heads from their parameters, without any model training or inference. We showcase the utility of MAPS for answering two types of questions: (a) given a predefined operation, mapping how strongly heads across the model implement it, and (b) given an attention head, inferring its salient functionality. Evaluating MAPS on 20 operations across 6 popular LLMs shows its estimations correlate with the head's outputs during inference and are causally linked to the model's predictions. Moreover, its mappings reveal attention heads of certain operations that were overlooked in previous studies, and valuable insights on function universality and architecture biases in LLMs. Next, we present an automatic pipeline and analysis that leverage MAPS to characterize the salient operations of a given head. Our pipeline produces plausible operation descriptions for most heads, as assessed by human judgment, while revealing diverse operations.

papers.title: Identifying a Circuit for Verb Conjugation in GPT-2
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 perform subject-verb agreement, and what is the minimal circuit responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a minimal circuit of attention heads in GPT-2 Small responsible for subject-verb agreement, showing that basic agreement relies on a small subset of heads while more complex linguistic features require larger circuits.
papers.conclusion: The study successfully isolated a circuit for verb conjugation in GPT-2, demonstrating that basic syntactic processing relies on a small subset of attention heads, but more complex linguistic features require larger, more distributed circuits.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 achieves high accuracy on subject-verb agreement across a range of controlled linguistic settings, including plural, negation, prefix, pronoun, tense, and irregular verbs.
A minimal circuit of 12 attention heads can achieve near-full model performance (0.65 accuracy vs. 0.70) on the base singular subject task.
For settings like plural, negation, and pronoun, circuit performance remains poor even after modest expansions, suggesting these features are more diffusely encoded or rely on non-attention mechanisms.
For settings like prefix, past tense, and irregular verbs, larger circuit expansions (up to 97 heads) achieve closer to full model performance (e.g., 0.82 vs. 0.93 for irregular verbs).
Analysis of attention patterns reveals categories of head functions, such as primary subject-anchors and conjunction-tracking, with some heads consistently important across settings.
papers.limitation:
Greedy search strategy may miss optimal circuits and combinatorial interactions.
Analysis focused exclusively on attention heads, omitting MLP components.
Path patching with resample ablation may still introduce unrealistic activation patterns.
Linguistic settings are bounded and artificial, not covering real-world complexity.
Manual categorization of head functions introduces subjectivity and limits reproducibility.
future_direction: MLP integration
Global optimization methods (e.g., ACDC) for circuit discovery
Cross-model comparisons to generalize findings
papers.abstract: I implement a procedure to isolate and interpret the sub-network (or "circuit") responsible for subject-verb agreement in GPT-2 Small. In this study, the model is given prompts where the subject is either singular (e.g. "Alice") or plural (e.g. "Alice and Bob"), and the task is to correctly predict the appropriate verb form ("walks" for singular subjects, "walk" for plural subjects). Using a series of techniques-including performance verification automatic circuit discovery via direct path patching, and direct logit attribution- I isolate a candidate circuit that contributes significantly to the model's correct verb conjugation. The results suggest that only a small fraction of the network's component-token pairs is needed to achieve near-model performance on the base task but substantially more for more complex settings.

papers.title: Responsibility Attribution for AI-Mediated Damages with Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What conception of causation should be used for responsibility attribution in AI-mediated damages, and how can mechanistic interpretability help in this context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that causation in legal responsibility attribution is best conceptualized as difference-making, and proposes mechanistic interpretability as a tool to identify difference-makers for AI-mediated damages, especially in high-risk scenarios.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability can enhance the ex-ante safety of opaque AI systems and aid in responsibility attribution, recommending its use in high-risk, high-stakes contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Causation for AI-mediated damages can be conceptualized as difference-making, with three types: inputs (type i), functional organization (type ii), and system history (type iii).
Classical XAI methods like LIME can identify type (i) difference-makers, while mechanistic interpretability is suited for type (ii).
For damages attributable to functional organization, liability may shift to deployers if they understand the system via MI.
Mechanistic interpretability should be required as a gold-standard for high-risk, high-stakes AI systems to improve ex-ante safety.
Legal rules should indemnify distant actors like data subjects in certain cases.
papers.limitation:
Type (i), (ii), and (iii) difference-makers are conceptually distinct but may be hard to disentangle in practice.
Mechanistic interpretability may be costly and infeasible to achieve for some systems.
Interpretability depends not only on system properties but also on stakeholders' cognitive abilities.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to generative AI systems.
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) raises profound ethical, moral, and legal challenges for society. In this paper, we focus on the legal challenge to adequately attribute responsibility for AI-mediated damages. In law, responsibility is usually attributed on the basis that a (human) actor is taking actions which cause harm or damage to some subject or property. While this analysis seems straightforward, it remains unclear (a) what conception of causation it relies on, (b) in what way this can be applied to attribute responsibility when human actions rely on the use of opaque AI systems, and (c) how liability for AI-mediated damages should be handled in practice. The current paper sets out to answer these questions. We shall argue that causation in the legal context is best conceptualized as difference-making. To determine relevant difference-makers for AI-mediated damages, we propose that explainable AI (XAI) methods may serve as important tools. Specifically, we argue, mechanistic interpretability (MI) is well-suited to increase the ex-ante safety of opaque AI systems.

papers.title: Opening the AI black box: program synthesis via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability be automated to distill learned algorithms from neural networks into Python code?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIPS, a fully automated method that distills learned algorithms from RNNs into Python code via mechanistic interpretability, complementing LLMs like GPT-4.
papers.conclusion: MIPS is a promising step towards automated mechanistic interpretability and can complement large language models in program synthesis, offering a path to more interpretable and trustworthy machine-learned models.
papers.key_findings:
MIPS solves 32 out of 62 algorithmic tasks, including 13 that GPT-4 Turbo does not solve.
MIPS can automatically discover integer and Boolean representations in RNN hidden states.
The method converts trained RNNs into finite state machines and then synthesizes Python code via symbolic regression.
MIPS does not rely on human training data such as code from GitHub.
The method demonstrates the feasibility of automated mechanistic interpretability for program synthesis.
papers.limitation:
Noise and non-linearity in the RNN can cause the integer autoencoder to fail, preventing symbolic regression.
The method assumes the RNN is a finite-state machine and may fail when continuous variables are used for computation.
future_direction: Scaling up the approach to larger models.
Handling continuous variables in the learned representations.
Improving robustness to noise and non-linearity.
papers.abstract: We present MIPS, a novel method for program synthesis based on automated mechanistic interpretability of neural networks trained to perform the desired task, auto-distilling the learned algorithm into Python code. We test MIPS on a benchmark of 62 algorithmic tasks that can be learned by an RNN and find it highly complementary to GPT-4: MIPS solves 32 of them, including 13 that are not solved by GPT-4 (which also solves 30). MIPS uses an integer autoencoder to convert the RNN into a finite state machine, then applies Boolean or integer symbolic regression to capture the learned algorithm. As opposed to large language models, this program synthesis technique makes no use of (and is therefore not limited by) human training data such as algorithms and code from GitHub. We discuss opportunities and challenges for scaling up this approach to make machine-learned models more interpretable and trustworthy.

papers.title: Evaluating Transformer's Ability to Learn Mildly Context-Sensitive Languages
papers.research_question: How well do Transformers learn mildly context-sensitive languages (MCSLs) from finite examples, in terms of generalizing to in-distribution data and extrapolating to longer strings? What kind of meaningful representations or patterns do the models learn?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically evaluates the Transformer's ability to learn a variety of mildly context-sensitive languages (MCSLs), finding that while they generalize well to in-distribution data, their ability to extrapolate to longer strings is worse than that of LSTMs. Analyses show the learned self-attention patterns model dependency relations and representations encode count information.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn mildly context-sensitive languages from finite examples and leverage self-attention to model dependency relations, but their extrapolation ability is limited compared to LSTMs. The learned patterns and behaviors provide insights into the models' linguistic capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers generalize well to unseen in-distribution data for MCSLs, performing comparably to LSTMs.
Transformers' ability to extrapolate to longer strings (out-of-distribution) is limited and generally worse than LSTMs.
Removing sinusoidal positional encoding in Transformer decoders (next character prediction tasks) can improve extrapolation ability.
Learned self-attention patterns often reflect the symbol dependency relations within the string (e.g., checkerboard patterns for crossing dependencies).
For the complex scramble language MIX, the learned representations encode count information for symbol occurrences, which may aid in solving the language.
papers.limitation:
The empirical study is bounded by a string length upper bound, so the dataset is bounded and might form a language with reduced complexity, weakening arguments about general learnability.
The roles of other heads, the feed-forward sublayer, etc. are not investigated, so it cannot be definitively said how self-attention directly contributed to inference.
papers.abstract: Despite the fact that Transformers perform well in NLP tasks, recent studies suggest that self-attention is theoretically limited in learning even some regular and context-free languages. These findings motivated us to think about their implications in modeling natural language, which is hypothesized to be mildly context-sensitive. We test the Transformer's ability to learn mildly context-sensitive languages of varying complexities, and find that they generalize well to unseen in-distribution data, but their ability to extrapolate to longer strings is worse than that of LSTMs. Our analyses show that the learned self-attention patterns and representations modeled dependency relations and demonstrated counting behavior, which may have helped the models solve the languages.

papers.title: Is logical analysis performed by transformers taking place in self-attention or in the fully connected part?
papers.research_question: Is the logical analysis in transformers done in the self-attention part or the fully connected layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that logical analysis can be performed within self-attention, and transformers can learn to use both self-attention and fully connected layers for logical operations.
papers.conclusion: The experiments underscore the flexibility of transformer architectures, i.e., their ability to perform tasks via multiple pathways and their combination, including an interesting symmetry in attention.
papers.key_findings:
Handcrafted solutions demonstrate that self-attention can perform logical analysis without fully connected layers.
Gradient descent can get stuck in undesirable local minima, but these can be avoided with Softmax or rescaling.
Experiments show transformers can learn to use self-attention for logical analysis, and a combined approach works best.
There is a symmetry in the attention mechanism allowing switching roles of k^T q and v.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic data (i.i.d. digit sequences) rather than real sentences.
The task is simple (predicting adjacent token categories); many more essential sequence processing tasks (e.g., memorization) are not studied.
future_direction: Studying more essential tasks in sequence processing, such as memorization tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformers architecture apply self-attention to tokens represented as vectors, before a fully connected (neuronal network) layer. These two parts can be layered many times. Traditionally, self-attention is seen as a mechanism for aggregating information before logical operations are performed by the fully connected layer. In this paper, we show, that quite counter-intuitively, the logical analysis can also be performed within the self-attention. For this we implement a handcrafted single-level encoder layer which performs the logical analysis within self-attention. We then study the scenario in which a one-level transformer model undergoes self-learning using gradient descent. We investigate whether the model utilizes fully connected layers or self-attention mechanisms for logical analysis when it has the choice. Given that gradient descent can become stuck at undesired zeros, we explicitly calculate these unwanted zeros and find ways to avoid them. We do all this in the context of predicting grammatical category pairs of adjacent tokens in a text. We believe that our findings have broader implications for understanding the potential logical operations performed by self-attention.

papers.title: Understanding Attention for Text Classification
papers.research_question: What are the underlying factors that influence the attention mechanism in text classification models, and how do attention scores and polarity scores impact model performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the internal mechanism of attention for text classification by examining token-level polarity scores and global attention scores, showing how hyperparameters like the scaling factor λ affect interpretability and model performance.
papers.conclusion: Examining both attention scores and polarity scores provides a better understanding of the attention mechanism, and hyperparameters like λ play a crucial role in interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention scores capture the global importance of tokens, while attention weights are local and instance-specific.
Polarity tokens (strongly associated with specific labels) tend to have larger attention scores and polarity scores when hyperparameters are properly set.
The scaling factor λ influences interpretability: when λ is too large, attention scores become less interpretable, but model performance remains good due to polarity scores.
The dot product V^T W affects the gap between attention scores of positive and negative tokens.
Empirical results on real datasets support the theoretical analysis, showing similar patterns for both scaled dot-product and additive attention.
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes a simple model architecture and balanced, symmetric datasets, which may not hold in practice.
future_direction: Examining the influence of using pre-trained word embeddings.
Examining the influence of using deep contextualized input encoders such as ELMo or BERT.
papers.abstract: Attention has been proven successful in many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Recently, many researchers started to investigate the interpretability of attention on NLP tasks. Many existing approaches focused on examining whether the local attention weights could reflect the importance of input representations. In this work, we present a study on understanding the internal mechanism of attention by looking into the gradient update process, checking its behavior when approaching a local minimum during training. We propose to analyze for each word token the following two quantities: its polarity score and its attention score, where the latter is a global assessment on the token's significance. We discuss conditions under which the attention mechanism may become more (or less) interpretable, and show how the interplay between the two quantities may impact the model performance. 1

papers.title: From Indirect Object Identification to Syllogisms: Exploring Binary Mechanisms in Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small handle binary truth values in syllogistic prompts, and what circuits are responsible for logical reasoning in these tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies circuits in GPT-2 small that handle syllogistic reasoning, uncovering binary mechanisms such as negation via negative attention heads and modulation via MLPs, and shows these circuits achieve high faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: By relating the findings on syllogistic reasoning circuits to prior IOI analysis, the paper provides new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs, contributing to a broader understanding of model reasoning and future mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Identified three distinct circuits for simple, opposite, and complex syllogisms in GPT-2 small.
Discovered a binary negation mechanism where negative truth heads produce the opposite token, aided by MLPs that rescale the residual stream.
Found empirical evidence for binary opposite tasks, showing the same attention heads flip their influence on logit difference between simple and opposite syllogisms.
Advanced interpretability of model components, detailing the roles of truth heads, negative truth heads, truth modulation heads, induction heads, and duplicate statement identifier heads.
Demonstrated that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model's performance on the simple syllogism task.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) can perform a wide range of tasks, and mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the components responsible for task completion to understand their behavior. Previous mechanistic interpretability research has primarily focused on linguistic tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI). In this paper, we investigate the ability of GPT-2 small to handle binary truth values by analyzing its behavior with syllogistic prompts, such as "Statement A is true. Statement B matches statement A. Statement B is'', which requires more complex logical reasoning compared to IOI. Through our analysis of several syllogism tasks of varying difficulty, we identify multiple circuits that explain GPT-2 small’s logical-reasoning capabilities and uncover binary mechanisms that facilitate task completion, including the ability to produce a negated token that does not appear in the input prompt through negative heads. Our evaluation using a faithfulness metric shows that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model’s performance. By relating our findings to IOI analysis, we provide new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs. We believe these insights contribute to a broader understanding of model reasoning and benefit future research in mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: When Do You Need Billions of Words of Pretraining Data?
papers.research_question: What knowledge or skills do Transformer LMs learn from large-scale pretraining that they cannot learn from less data, and how much pretraining data is required to learn different linguistic features?
papers.core_contribution: Linguistic features are learned with relatively little pretraining data (10M-100M words), while commonsense knowledge and downstream NLU task performance require billions of words.
papers.conclusion: Linguistic features are mostly learnable with 100M words of data, while NLU task performance requires far more data, suggesting that other forms of knowledge (e.g., commonsense) are the major drivers of improvements in large pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic features (syntactic and semantic) are mostly learnable with 100M words of pretraining data.
Commonsense knowledge, as measured by the Winograd task, requires more data and improves up to 30B words.
Performance on NLU tasks (SuperGLUE) requires billions of words and does not saturate at 30B words.
There is variation in data needs for different linguistic phenomena: agreement phenomena are learned quickly, while wh-dependencies and quantifiers require more data or are not learned effectively.
The accessibility of features, as measured by minimum description length probing, does not show a different trend from classifier probing.
papers.limitation:
The Winograd task results are somewhat noisy due to well-known idiosyncrasies of the task.
The MDL method may not adequately differentiate between feature information and accessibility, as the overall codelength predominantly reflects the decrease in loss.
The experiments focus mainly on linguistic knowledge, so additional work is needed to give a more complete picture of the acquisition of commonsense knowledge.
future_direction: Use causal probing methods like amnesic probing to understand what causes NLU task performance to improve with large quantities of data.
Understand the differences between learning curves for various linguistic features, e.g., whether some features acquired earlier bootstrap knowledge of other features.
Extend the investigation to other pretraining settings, model architectures, pretraining tasks, and data domains to close the gap between models and human learners.
papers.abstract: NLP is currently dominated by general-purpose pretrained language models like RoBERTa, which achieve strong performance on NLU tasks through pretraining on billions of words. But what exact knowledge or skills do Transformer LMs learn from large-scale pretraining that they cannot learn from less data? We adopt four probing methods---classifier probing, information-theoretic probing, unsupervised relative acceptability judgment, and fine-tuning on NLU tasks---and draw learning curves that track the growth of these different measures of linguistic ability with respect to pretraining data volume using the MiniBERTas, a group of RoBERTa models pretrained on 1M, 10M, 100M and 1B words. We find that LMs require only about 10M or 100M words to learn representations that reliably encode most syntactic and semantic features we test. A much larger quantity of data is needed in order to acquire enough commonsense knowledge and other skills required to master typical downstream NLU tasks. The results suggest that, while the ability to encode linguistic features is almost certainly necessary for language understanding, it is likely that other forms of knowledge are the major drivers of recent improvements in language understanding among large pretrained models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Models: Circuit-Level Analysis and Causal Validation
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models internally process and transform information during the denoising procedure, and what are the computational circuits and mechanisms underlying image generation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a quantitative circuit-level analysis framework for diffusion models, revealing systematic algorithmic differences in how they process synthetic versus naturalistic data, identifying specialized attention mechanisms, and providing causal validation through intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes the first comprehensive circuit-level analysis of diffusion models, providing quantitative foundations for mechanistic interpretability and revealing systematic algorithmic differences between synthetic and naturalistic data processing with implications for model control and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Real-world face processing requires circuits with measurably higher computational complexity than synthetic data processing, though with variability across model initializations.
Eight functionally distinct attention mechanisms with specialized computational roles (e.g., edge detection, texture analysis, semantic understanding) were identified and quantified.
Temporal activation analysis reveals distinct processing phases across the denoising process, with some attention heads specializing in early structure formation and others in detail refinement.
Intervention analysis identifies critical computational bottlenecks, with targeted ablations producing performance degradation from 25.6% to 153.8%.
Circuit transferability varies with abstraction level and temporal phase, suggesting a hierarchical organization of fundamental and domain-specific computations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on facial image generation using synthetic and CelebA datasets, which may limit generalizability to other image domains.
The model used is a 262M parameter architecture, substantially smaller than state-of-the-art diffusion models, which may limit the discovery of emergent capabilities and circuit complexity present in larger models.
While intervention analysis provides evidence for circuit functionality, more sophisticated causal analysis methods could strengthen mechanistic claims.
The correlation between attention head entropy and peak activation timing did not reach statistical significance, suggesting head specialization is multidimensional.
future_direction: Extending the circuit analysis methodologies to larger-scale diffusion models and diverse generation tasks.
Developing more sophisticated causal analysis techniques for understanding generative model computation.
Extending the methodologies to text-to-image generation and other cross-modal tasks.
papers.abstract: We present a quantitative circuit-level analysis of diffusion models, establishing computational pathways and mechanistic principles underlying image generation processes. Through systematic intervention experiments across 2,000 synthetic and 2,000 CelebA facial images, we discover fundamental algorithmic differences in how diffusion architectures process synthetic versus naturalistic data distributions. Our investigation reveals that real-world face processing requires circuits with measurably higher computational complexity (complexity ratio = 1.084 plus/minus 0.008, p < 0.001), exhibiting distinct attention specialization patterns with entropy divergence ranging from 0.015 to 0.166 across denoising timesteps. We identify eight functionally distinct attention mechanisms showing specialized computational roles: edge detection (entropy = 3.18 plus/minus 0.12), texture analysis (entropy = 4.16 plus/minus 0.08), and semantic understanding (entropy = 2.67 plus/minus 0.15). Intervention analysis demonstrates critical computational bottlenecks where targeted ablations produce 25.6% to 128.3% performance degradation, providing causal evidence for identified circuit functions. These findings establish quantitative foundations for algorithmic understanding and control of generative model behavior through mechanistic intervention strategies.

papers.title: Visualizing Attention in Transformer-Based Language Representation\n Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an open-source tool for visualizing multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based language models, extending earlier work by adding model-level and neuron-level views.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a visualization tool for attention in Transformer models and demonstrates its utility through use cases on GPT-2 and BERT.
papers.key_findings:
The tool can detect model bias, such as gender bias in coreference resolution in GPT-2, by visualizing attention patterns that link pronouns to gender-stereotyped nouns.
The model view identifies recurring attention patterns, including null attention to the first token, suggesting potential improvements for model interpretability.
The neuron view links individual neurons to attention behaviors, such as specific neurons influencing distance-decaying attention patterns, enabling potential human intervention.
future_direction: Evaluate empirically how attention impacts model predictions across a range of tasks.
Integrate the three views into a unified interface.
Visualize the value vectors in addition to the queries and keys.
papers.abstract:
We present an open-source tool for visualizing multi-head self-attention in
Transformer-based language representation models. The tool extends earlier work
by visualizing attention at three levels of granularity: the attention-head
level, the model level, and the neuron level. We describe how each of these
views can help to interpret the model, and we demonstrate the tool on the BERT
model and the OpenAI GPT-2 model. We also present three use cases for analyzing
GPT-2: detecting model bias, identifying recurring patterns, and linking
neurons to model behavior.

papers.title: Is Attention Interpretable?
papers.research_question: Does attention provide a faithful explanation for model decisions by identifying important input components?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not reliably interpretable as importance indicators; they are only noisy predictors of input components' importance to the model.
papers.conclusion: Attention is not an optimal method of identifying which attended elements are responsible for an output; as an importance ranking, it fails to explain model decisions.
papers.key_findings:
The highest attention weight often has a larger impact than a random weight, but there are many cases where the impact is similar.
Attention weights often fail to identify the minimal set of representations that are important for the model's decision.
Gradient-based rankings of attention weights often predict their effects better than their magnitudes.
The scope of contextualization (e.g., RNN vs. convolutional encoders) affects how well attention indicates importance.
In encoderless models, attention magnitudes are more helpful, but still not optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on text classification, which may not generalize to tasks with larger output spaces (e.g., language modeling).
Reliance on argmax decision flips as a measure of importance, which might be too coarse.
Only evaluated on specific attention functions (additive attention) and final layers; other variants and lower layers might behave differently.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other tasks and models with larger output spaces.
Develop better, more informative importance rankings.
Align models with human feedback for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have recently boosted performance on a range of NLP tasks. Because attention layers explicitly weight input components' representations, it is also often assumed that attention can be used to identify information that models found important (e.g., specific contextualized word tokens). We test whether that assumption holds by manipulating attention weights in already-trained text classification models and analyzing the resulting differences in their predictions. While we observe some ways in which higher attention weights correlate with greater impact on model predictions, we also find many ways in which this does not hold, i.e., where gradient-based rankings of attention weights better predict their effects than their magnitudes. We conclude that while attention noisily predicts input components' overall importance to a model, it is by no means a fail-safe indicator. 1

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: Attention is not Explanation
papers.research_question: To what extent do attention weights provide meaningful explanations for model predictions in neural NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that standard attention modules in neural NLP models do not provide meaningful explanations for predictions, as attention weights correlate poorly with feature importance measures and can be adversarially manipulated without changing predictions.
papers.conclusion: Standard attention modules do not provide meaningful explanations for model predictions and should not be treated as though they do.
papers.key_findings:
Learned attention weights are frequently uncorrelated with gradient-based and leave-one-out measures of feature importance.
One can construct adversarial attention distributions that are maximally different from the original but yield equivalent predictions.
Randomly permuting attention weights often induces only minimal changes in model output.
Attention weights in simple feedforward (average) encoders show better correlation with feature importance than those in BiLSTM encoders.
For complex encoders like BiLSTM, attention weights are not reliable explanations and should not be treated as such.
papers.limitation:
The Kendall τ correlation measure may be depressed by noise from irrelevant features, potentially affecting the assessment of attention-feature importance correlation.
The study only considered a handful of attention variants and encoder architectures, limiting generalizability.
The work did not consider seq2seq tasks, which are common for attention models.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to seq2seq tasks such as machine translation.
Develop more principled attention mechanisms that provide faithful explanations.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have seen wide adoption in neural NLP models. In addition to improving predictive performance, these are often touted as affording transparency: models equipped with attention provide a distribution over attended-to input units, and this is often presented (at least implicitly) as communicating the relative importance of inputs. However, it is unclear what relationship exists between attention weights and model outputs. In this work, we perform extensive experiments across a variety of NLP tasks that aim to assess the degree to which attention weights provide meaningful `explanations' for predictions. We find that they largely do not. For example, learned attention weights are frequently uncorrelated with gradient-based measures of feature importance, and one can identify very different attention distributions that nonetheless yield equivalent predictions. Our findings show that standard attention modules do not provide meaningful explanations and should not be treated as though they do. Code for all experiments is available at https://github.com/successar/AttentionExplanation.

papers.title: The Unstoppable Rise of Computational Linguistics in Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How has the nature of language influenced the development of neural network architectures, and what are the future challenges?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the success of deep learning in NLP stems from incorporating computational linguistic insights, such as variable binding and structured representations, and that Transformer is an induced-structure model that captures these, leading to predictions about future challenges.
papers.conclusion: The nature of language has fundamentally influenced deep learning architectures, leading to models like Transformer that use bag-of-vector representations to capture unbounded structured representations, but many hand-coded aspects remain, and inducing entities and levels is a key future challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Vector-space representations alone are inadequate for language; structured representations are necessary.
Attention-based models introduce variable binding, allowing them to represent structured relationships.
Transformer is not a sequence model but an induced-structure model that can capture linguistic relations.
Bag-of-vector representations in Transformer are nonparametric and exchangeable, enabling unbounded representations.
Future challenges include inducing entities and levels of representation from data.
future_direction: Inducing entities at a given level of representation
Inducing the levels of representation themselves
Developing new neural network architectures that can learn entities and levels from data
papers.abstract: In this paper, we trace the history of neural networks applied to natural language understanding tasks, and identify key contributions which the nature of language has made to the development of neural network architectures. We focus on the importance of variable binding and its instantiation in attention-based models, and argue that Transformer is not a sequence model but an induced-structure model. This perspective leads to predictions of the challenges facing research in deep learning architectures for natural language understanding.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: Grammatical Gender Affects Bilinguals’ Conceptual Gender: Implications for Linguistic Relativity and Decision Making~!2008-03-31~!2008-10-13~!2008-11-26~!
papers.abstract: We used a non-linguistic gender attribution task to determine how French and Spanish grammatical gender affects bilinguals' conceptual gender. French-English and Spanish-English bilingual, as well as English monolingual adults were asked to assign a male or female voice to 32 color drawings depicting people, animals, and common objects. French-English and Spanish-English bilinguals classified items according to French and Spanish grammatical gender respectively. This effect was replicated for French-English bilinguals on those items whose grammatical gender was opposite in French and Spanish. Unexpectedly, Spanish gender similarly affected classifications by Spanish-English and English-Spanish bilinguals, as well as English monolinguals. We discuss how grammatical gender, possible covariates, and the order of L1 and L2 acquisition, affect conceptual gender as well as implications for decision making.

papers.title: Grammatical gender processing in bilinguals: An analytic review
papers.abstract: In this review article, we analyze how grammatical gender is represented and processed in the bilingual mind. To that end, we review the data from 13 existing behavioral studies of mainly late second language (L2) learners on the so-called gender congruency (GC) effect (facilitated processing for translation equivalents with the same gender, in comparison to those with a different gender) in L2 production and comprehension. The majority of the results showed a GC effect, regardless of the type of language involved. However, the state of cognateness of the target nouns, as well as the similarity between the gender systems of the bilingual speakers and their L2 proficiency, modulated the results. Interestingly, a gender agreement context is not required in order to observe gender effects, in that they are also observed with bare nouns. Overall, the findings support an integrative view of bilingual gender representation, with competitive and inhibitory processes at different levels of language processing underlying cross-language GC effects.

papers.title: Revisiting Masculine and Feminine Grammatical Gender in Spanish: Linguistic, Psycholinguistic, and Neurolinguistic Evidence
papers.abstract: Research on grammatical gender processing has generally assumed that grammatical gender can be treated as a uniform construct, resulting in a body of literature in which different gender classes are collapsed into single analysis. The present work reviews linguistic, psycholinguistic, and neurolinguistic research on grammatical gender from different methodologies and across different profiles of Spanish speakers. Specifically, we examine distributional asymmetries between masculine and feminine grammatical gender, the resulting biases in gender assignment, and the consequences of these assignment strategies on gender expectancy and processing.
